title: UK Population Distribution & a Major UK City

claims_checked.claim: The UK's population is just over 67 million
claims_checked.source_says: ONS mid-2024 estimate is 69.3 million — the lesson figure is ~3% low

claims_checked.claim: Greater London alone holds over 9 million people
claims_checked.source_says: GLA 2024 estimate ~9.09 million — claim is accurate

claims_checked.claim: Manchester city itself has around 560,000 residents
claims_checked.source_says: 2021 Census: 551,900; slight overstatement but within acceptable range for GCSE rounding

claims_checked.claim: The wider Greater Manchester metropolitan region has around 2.9 million
claims_checked.source_says: Greater Manchester population is ~3.01 million in 2024; 2.9m was closer to 2011-era figures

claims_checked.claim: Manchester is the second-largest urban area in the UK after London
claims_checked.source_says: Standard geographical classification; Greater Manchester is the second-largest urban area in the UK by population

claims_checked.claim: Manchester Airport is the third-busiest in the UK after Heathrow and Gatwick, with direct flights to over 200 destinations
claims_checked.source_says: Manchester is consistently the third-busiest UK airport. 200+ destination claim is plausible and commonly cited in airport materials

claims_checked.claim: The Manchester Ship Canal, opened in 1894
claims_checked.source_says: Opened to traffic 1 January 1894; officially opened by Queen Victoria 21 May 1894

claims_checked.claim: Manchester is the BBC's second hub at MediaCityUK in Salford
claims_checked.source_says: MediaCityUK Salford is BBC's main hub outside London, operational since 2011

claims_checked.claim: The 2017 opening of the BBC at MediaCityUK pulled hundreds of broadcasters out of London
claims_checked.source_says: BBC began operations at MediaCityUK in 2011, not 2017. The major move of BBC Sport and BBC Breakfast was 2011-2012

notes: UK population figure (67m) is now ~3% too low; 'BBC 2017' date is wrong by 6 years. Both are addressable with a data refresh.

title: Plate Margins & Why People Stay

claims_checked.claim: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge splits the Atlantic at about 2 cm a year
claims_checked.source_says: USGS/Wikipedia: average spreading rate ~2.5 cm/year, ranging from 2-5 cm/year depending on segment. '2 cm' is at the low end but not wrong as a GCSE simplification

claims_checked.claim: The Andes formed where the Nazca Plate is being subducted beneath the South American Plate
claims_checked.source_says: Confirmed by USGS and multiple academic sources

claims_checked.claim: India is still pushing into Eurasia at about 5 cm a year
claims_checked.source_says: Current convergence rate ~4-5 cm/yr — consistent with claim

claims_checked.claim: The San Andreas Fault: the Pacific Plate is sliding north past the North American Plate at about 5 cm a year
claims_checked.source_says: Movement rate is 4-6 cm/year; 5 cm is an accurate GCSE-level figure

claims_checked.claim: Mount St Helens (USA, 1980) is a textbook example [of a destructive eruption]
claims_checked.source_says: Mt St Helens sits on a destructive margin (Juan de Fuca subducting under North American plate) — well established

claims_checked.claim: Around 800 million people live within range of an active volcano
claims_checked.source_says: Various sources cite 500 million to 800 million within ~100km of a Holocene volcano. GCSE-level estimate is in range

notes: Solid physical geography content. The 2 cm/year Mid-Atlantic Ridge rate is at the low end but defensible for GCSE. No significant factual errors.

title: Hot Deserts: Conditions, Adaptations & Opportunities

claims_checked.claim: Hot deserts receive less than 250 mm of rainfall a year
claims_checked.source_says: Standard geographic definition — well established

claims_checked.claim: Deserts lie in two bands at around 30° north and south of the equator
claims_checked.source_says: Subtropical high pressure belt at ~30° — correct physical geography

claims_checked.claim: Acacia trees can reach 30 metres down to the water table
claims_checked.source_says: Some acacia species have roots recorded at 30-40m depth. This figure appears in textbooks but primary citations are hard to pin down. Plausible but may be a high-end example presented as typical

claims_checked.claim: Camels can drink up to 100 litres of water in 10 minutes
claims_checked.source_says: Natural History Museum and multiple zoological sources confirm ~100 litres in one session (often cited as 10-15 minutes)

claims_checked.claim: A camel can lose up to 25% of its body water without ill effects
claims_checked.source_says: Scientific literature confirms camels can withstand 25%+ body-water loss (vs ~10% in humans)

claims_checked.claim: Australia's Western Desert covers around 270,000 km², similar in size to the UK
claims_checked.source_says: The Western Desert cultural bloc covers ~600,000-670,000 km². The 'Western Desert' as a geographic/geological region is typically cited at ~250,000-600,000 km² depending on boundaries used. UK is ~244,000 km². The 270,000 km² figure is at the very low end and the 'similar to UK' comparison is approximately true only on a restricted definition. Many sources give larger figures.

claims_checked.claim: Indigenous Aboriginal peoples have lived there for over 40,000 years
claims_checked.source_says: Most recent evidence supports 50,000+ years of Indigenous Australian presence; 40,000 years is a conservative/older figure but not incorrect

notes: Generally accurate. The Western Desert size (270,000 km²) is on the low end of published estimates; the exact figure depends on which boundary definition is used. Not a serious error for GCSE.

title: Migration, Inequality & UK Urban Challenges

claims_checked.claim: The 2021 census found that around 33% of Manchester city residents were born outside the UK
claims_checked.source_says: 2021 Census: 31.4% of Manchester residents were born outside the UK (173,208 out of 551,900). The lesson overstates by ~1.6 percentage points, citing 33% when the actual figure is 31.4%. Not a rounding issue — the lesson explicitly attributes this to the '2021 census'.

claims_checked.claim: Manchester's four universities have around 100,000 students between them, with the University of Manchester alone hosting roughly 45,000
claims_checked.source_says: University of Manchester had 46,915 students in 2023-24 — the 45,000 figure is slightly low but acceptable for GCSE rounding. The four-university 100,000 total is a reasonable estimate.

claims_checked.claim: Net migration in 2023 was around 685,000 — a record figure
claims_checked.source_says: 685,000 is the ONS provisional figure for year-ending December 2023, but the actual record was ~906,000 for year-ending June 2023 (later revised). Calling 685,000 a 'record' is misleading — it was high but the peak was higher. However, at the time of writing (pre-revision) this may have been the best available figure.

notes: The 33% foreign-born figure is wrong — Census shows 31.4%. This is attributed directly to the 2021 Census so is verifiably incorrect. The migration figure context (calling it a 'record') is also misleading since the true peak was considerably higher.

title: Uneven Global Development

claims_checked.claim: Average life expectancy is 84 years in Switzerland and 60 in Mozambique
claims_checked.source_says: Switzerland 2024: ~84.4 years (correct). Mozambique 2024: ~63.8 years — the lesson states 60 which is ~4 years too low; Mozambique's life expectancy has risen noticeably in recent years.

claims_checked.claim: Norway and Switzerland top the HDI
claims_checked.source_says: UNDP HDR 2023/24: Switzerland and Norway are both at 0.970, among the very top — accurate

claims_checked.claim: China now produces about 18% of global GDP
claims_checked.source_says: China's nominal GDP share is ~17-18% in 2024; in PPP terms ~19%. The 18% claim is in the correct range.

claims_checked.claim: India has the world's fifth-largest economy
claims_checked.source_says: India was 5th largest in 2024 by nominal GDP. By 2026 estimates it may be 4th or 6th depending on revisions. Was accurate when written.

claims_checked.claim: India has overtaken China as the world's most populous country
claims_checked.source_says: India overtook China as world's most populous country in 2023 — confirmed by UN

claims_checked.claim: The UN accepted the 17 Sustainable Development Goals in 2015
claims_checked.source_says: SDGs adopted by UN member states in September 2015 — accurate

notes: Mozambique life expectancy stated as 60 but is now ~64. A student could be penalised in an exam for repeating this outdated figure if an examiner checks. The comparison with Switzerland remains a valid point of contrast.

title: Climate Change Causes & Evidence

claims_checked.claim: The Quaternary period covers the last 2.6 million years
claims_checked.source_says: Standard geological classification — correct

claims_checked.claim: The current interglacial began around 11,700 years ago
claims_checked.source_says: Holocene started ~11,700 years ago — accurate

claims_checked.claim: The Maunder Minimum from 1645–1715 is linked with the coldest part of the Little Ice Age
claims_checked.source_says: Well-established link between Maunder Minimum (low solar activity) and cold period — correct

claims_checked.claim: Mount Pinatubo in 1991 caused global temperatures to dip by around 0.5°C in the year following
claims_checked.source_says: USGS: cooling peaked at ~0.5°C about 18 months after eruption — accurate

claims_checked.claim: The Antarctic Vostok core is over 3.6km long
claims_checked.source_says: Vostok core reached 3,623 m — over 3.6 km is accurate

claims_checked.claim: Ice cores let scientists read CO2 levels and temperatures going back over 800,000 years
claims_checked.source_says: EPICA Dome C core covers ~800,000 years (Vostok is ~420,000 years — the 800,000 years refers to the EPICA core, not Vostok specifically). The claim is accurate for ice cores in general.

claims_checked.claim: Atmospheric CO2 has risen from around 280 ppm in 1850 to over 420 ppm today
claims_checked.source_says: NOAA 2024: global average CO2 was 422.8 ppm — the claim is accurate

claims_checked.claim: Global temperatures are roughly 1.1°C higher than the 1850–1900 baseline
claims_checked.source_says: IPCC AR6 cited 1.1°C for 2011-2020 average; 2024 alone was ~1.35°C above baseline. The 1.1°C figure is the well-cited AR6 number and remains acceptable for GCSE.

claims_checked.claim: Sea levels have risen roughly 21–24 cm since 1900
claims_checked.source_says: NOAA and Smithsonian: ~20-23 cm since 1900. The range given in the lesson is accurate.

notes: Accurate, well-cited content. The 1.1°C warming figure is the established AR6 reference and still appropriate for GCSE even though 2024 individually exceeded it. No material errors.

title: Energy Futures: Reducing Reliance on Fossil Fuels

claims_checked.claim: Fossil fuels are still 80% of the world's primary energy supply
claims_checked.source_says: IEA World Energy Outlook 2023/24: fossil fuels account for ~80% of primary energy — this figure is correct for the time of writing, though the proportion is slowly declining

claims_checked.claim: The Athabasca tar sands of Alberta produce around 3 million barrels a day
claims_checked.source_says: Alberta oil sands production was ~3.5 million bpd in 2024; Alberta.ca reports projections around 5+ million bpd including all deposits. The '3 million' figure is below actual production levels and appears to be based on ~2015 figures.

claims_checked.claim: Producing one barrel of tar-sand oil emits 3× more CO₂ than conventional oil
claims_checked.source_says: Various lifecycle analyses put tar-sand emissions at 2-4× conventional oil well-to-wheel. 3× is a commonly cited midpoint figure — acceptable

claims_checked.claim: Solar PV costs fell 90% from 2010 to 2024
claims_checked.source_says: IRENA 2024: solar LCOE fell 90% from 2010 to 2024 — exact match

claims_checked.claim: The UK alone generating about 30% of electricity from wind in 2024
claims_checked.source_says: NESO and Ember: wind generated ~29-30% of UK electricity in 2024, becoming the UK's top source — accurate

claims_checked.claim: Three Gorges Dam displaced 1.3 million people
claims_checked.source_says: Official Chinese government figure is 1.3 million; some critics say up to 1.9 million. The 1.3 million figure is the standard cited number.

claims_checked.claim: The average UK person has a carbon footprint of about 7 tonnes CO₂ per year
claims_checked.source_says: UK consumption-based emissions per capita are roughly 7-8 tonnes CO₂e/year depending on methodology. The 7 tonne figure is at the lower end but commonly cited.

notes: The Athabasca tar sands production figure (3 million bpd) is now notably low — actual production exceeded 3.5 million bpd in 2024 and is growing. The error is >20% off current reality, meeting HIGH threshold. All other claims are sound.

title: Presenting & Analysing Fieldwork Data

claims_checked.claim: Median is useful for skewed data such as pebble size, where one boulder can pull the mean
claims_checked.source_says: Standard statistical methodology — accurate

claims_checked.claim: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
claims_checked.source_says: Standard formula — correct

claims_checked.claim: GIS tools like Esri ArcGIS Online or Digimap
claims_checked.source_says: Both are legitimate, widely-used GIS platforms used in UK schools — accurate

claims_checked.claim: Choropleth maps shade areas by value; flow-line maps use thick arrows to show movement
claims_checked.source_says: Standard geographic data presentation definitions — accurate

notes: This lesson is primarily methodological (fieldwork skills) rather than factual geography. No statistics, case studies or data figures to verify. Content is accurate and matches Edexcel fieldwork methodology guidance.
